snip.t: A pleural effusion is an abnormal collection of fluid in the pleural space (between the visceral and parietal pleura).
Pleura (visceral & parietal) – serous membrane with rich lymphatics.: Invasion produces malignant pleural effusion; pleural seeding is a common route for distant metastasis.
Pleural membranes – visceral and parietal pleura with potential space: Inflammation can extend to the pleura → pleuritic pain, pleural rub, and effusion/empyema if fluid accumulates.
Symptoms: progressive dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain (may disappear as fluid separates the pleura), dry cough; plus symptoms of the cause (fever, weight loss, orthopnoea).

Pleural membranes (visceral pleura, parietal pleura): Extension of infection through the visceral pleura can produce empyema or bronchopleural fistula; knowledge of pleural anatomy guides drainage decisions.
Extension through visceral pleura → Empyema or bronchopleural fistula

Lymphatic drainage of the pleura – stomata on parietal pleura, subpleural lymphatics: Asbestos fibres migrate to pleural space, provoke chronic inflammation → pleural plaques, diffuse thickening, and mesothelioma.
Tumour angiogenesis (VEGF ↑) + matrix degradation (MMPs) → local invasion of bronchial wall, vessels, pleura

qs.q: What is considered the optimal method for obtaining pleural biopsies to ensure the best diagnostic results by allowing direct visualization of the pleura?
qs.e: The best results are obtained from video-assisted thoracoscopy, allowing the operator to visualise the pleura and guide the biopsy directly. Blind percutaneous biopsy lacks this direct visual control.

qs.q: Which immunohistochemical marker is highly sensitive and specific for distinguishing malignant mesothelioma from metastatic adenocarcinoma to the pleura?
qs.e: Calretinin, along with WT-1 and D2-40, are common markers for malignant mesothelioma. In contrast, TTF-1 (thyroid transcription factor-1) and CEA (carcinoembryonic antigen) are typically positive in adenocarcinomas, especially those of pulmonary origin.
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - October 16, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: Which immunohistochemical marker is most useful in distinguishing malignant mesothelioma from metastatic adenocarcinoma to the pleura?
qs.e: WT-1 (Wilms tumor 1) is typically positive in malignant mesothelioma and negative in most metastatic adenocarcinomas. CK7 can be positive in both, CK20 is more characteristic of adenocarcinoma, and TTF-1 is typically positive in lung adenocarcinoma.
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - October 9, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: Which immunohistochemical marker distinguishes malignant mesothelioma from metastatic adenocarcinoma to the pleura?
qs.e: Calretinin is a marker that is typically positive in malignant mesothelioma and negative in most metastatic adenocarcinomas to the pleura. CK7 is often positive in both, CK20 and TTF-1 are more typically associated with adenocarcinomas, particularly those of the lung or gastrointestinal tract.
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - October 2, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 70-year-old bedridden woman (post-CVA, 5 weeks) has sudden dyspnea then 2 days later develops left-sided pleuritic chest pain. Imaging shows a wedge-shaped hemorrhagic area at the left lower lobe pleura. Most likely finding in her pulmonary arteries?
qs.e: Immobility → DVT → pulmonary thromboembolism → wedge-shaped hemorrhagic infarct at the pleural base. Pleuritic chest pain indicates pleural involvement by the infarct.

es.q: A 65-year-old former shipyard worker presents with dyspnea. He has a significant history of asbestos exposure. a) Identify the most common manifestation of asbestos exposure in the pleura. (1 mark) b) List two distinct lung cancer risks significantly increased by asbestos exposure. (2 marks) c) Desc
es.m: a) The most common manifestation of asbestos exposure in the pleura is pleural plaques. b) Asbestos exposure significantly increases the risk of: 1) Lung cancer (approximately 5 times). 2) Malignant mesothelioma (over 1000 times). c) Asbestosis primarily affects the lower lobes of the lungs.
es.s: Respiratory System Pathology 1A — Practice Questions — Essay Questions

es.q: A long-term construction worker is suspected of having asbestos exposure. Describe the most common manifestation of asbestos exposure in the lungs and pleura, its typical symptomatic presentation, and critically compare the lung cancer risk associated with asbestos exposure versus Coal Worker's Pneu
es.m: The most common manifestation of asbestos exposure is pleural plaques, which are usually asymptomatic and primarily affect the lower lobes of the lungs. Asbestos exposure significantly increases lung cancer risk (5x) and carries a very high risk of malignant mesothelioma (>1000x). In contrast, Coal Worker's Pneumoconiosis (CWP) does not increase lung cancer risk.
es.s: Respiratory System Pathology 1A — Practice Questions — Essay Questions

es.q: A 65-year-old former shipyard worker presents with respiratory symptoms. In the context of asbestos exposure, identify its most common manifestation in the lungs or pleura, and name two distinct malignant conditions for which asbestos is a significant risk factor.
es.m: The most common manifestation of asbestos exposure in the lungs or pleura are pleural plaques, which are usually asymptomatic. Two distinct malignant conditions for which asbestos exposure is a significant risk factor are lung cancer and malignant mesothelioma.
es.s: Respiratory System Pathology 1A — Practice Questions — Essay Questions

es.q: A patient with a history of occupational exposure to asbestos presents with imaging findings of fibrous thickening on the pleura. What is the most common manifestation of asbestos exposure, and which asbestos-related pathology carries a significantly increased risk of malignant mesothelioma?
es.m: The most common manifestation of asbestos exposure is pleural plaques, which are usually asymptomatic. Asbestos exposure significantly increases the risk of malignant mesothelioma (more than 1000x).
es.s: Respiratory System Pathology 1A — Practice Questions — Essay Questions

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The pleura are thin serous membranes covering the lungs and lining the chest wall, creating a lubricated, negative-pressure space that allows smooth lung expansion during breathing.

sections.p: The pleura consist of visceral and parietal layers that together form a potential space. They reduce friction and maintain negative intrapleural pressure, essential for efficient ventilation.
b: Visceral pleura covers lung surface; parietal lines chest wall, diaphragm, mediastinum

sections.p: The pleural cavity lies between the two pleural layers, extending from the thoracic inlet to the diaphragm. The mediastinal pleura attaches to the pericardium and esophagus.
b: Visceral pleura attaches to lung surface; parietal pleura attaches to chest wall

sections.p: The pleural space is adjacent to the mediastinum, diaphragm, and thoracic cavity. It communicates with the pericardial space via the mediastinal pleura.
b: Parietal pleura contacts ribs, intercostal muscles, and diaphragm

sections.p: The pleura receive blood from the intercostal arteries (parietal) and pulmonary arteries (visceral).
Sensory innervation comes from intercostal nerves (parietal) and phrenic nerve (diaphragmatic pleura).
The pleura create a low-friction, negative-pressure environment that allows lungs to expand and contract smoothly during breathing.
Pleural disease arises when fluid, air, or infection enters the pleural space, disrupting pressure balance and lung expansion. Common causes include infection, malignancy, heart failure, and trauma.

t.b: Shows fluid level or lung collapse; indicates effusion or pneumothorax.
Obtains fluid for cytology, culture, and biochemical analysis; confirms diagnosis.
Detects fluid, guides aspiration, and assesses pleural thickening.

sections.p: Remember that pleural effusion is a collection of fluid between visceral and parietal pleura. The pleural space is a potential space; any fluid or air breaks the potentiality.
b: Effusion causes dyspnea, pleuritic pain, and decreased breath sounds

sections.p: Treat underlying cause (e.g., antibiotics for infection, diuretics for heart failure). Supportive care includes thoracentesis or chest tube for large effusions or pneumothorax.
Pneumothorax (air in pleural space) and pericardial effusion (fluid around heart).
Small effusions may be occult on chest X‑ray; ultrasound is more sensitive.
Urgent care needed if sudden dyspnea, chest pain, or hemodynamic instability suggestive of tension pneumothorax or massive effusion.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe shortness of breath, chest pain, or hemodynamic instability indicating tension pneumothorax or massive effusion

faq.a: Fluid accumulation due to increased capillary permeability, decreased oncotic pressure, or lymphatic obstruction.

faq.q: How is a pleural effusion diagnosed?
faq.a: Chest X‑ray, ultrasound, and thoracentesis with fluid analysis.

faq.q: What is the difference between pleural effusion and pneumothorax?
faq.a: Effusion is fluid; pneumothorax is air in the pleural space.
